title: By my own hands
hookLine: a hadith: no one eats better food than what they earn with their own hands (Bukhari)

lines: WHAT MAKES A MEAL TASTE BETTER?
THE WORK OF ONE'S OWN HANDS.
cards: What makes one meal taste better than another? Salt, sure. Hunger.
Good company. Here's another answer, from a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, kept in the collection of al-Bukhari.
In paraphrase: no one has ever eaten better food than what they eat from the work of their own hands. And then, to make the point, he names a king.
David, the prophet of God, he says, used to eat from the work of his own hands. A king, who could have had anything brought to him, earning his bread.

teach.b: First, the claim. The saying doesn't say rich food, or holy food, or food eaten in a mosque. It says better food is what you earn yourself.
The value isn't in the plate. It's in the hands that paid for it. Second, the king.
The Qur'an tells of David as a prophet and a ruler, and also as a craftsman.
It says God made iron soft for him and told him to make coats of mail, measuring the links with care, and to do good work.
So when the hadith says David ate from the work of his hands, it points to a ruler who kept a trade. Third, the dignity in it.

teach.h: A ROPE AND A BUNDLE OF FIREWOOD.
teach.b: Another saying in al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: it's better for one of you to take a rope, bring a bundle of firewood on your back and sell it, than to go and beg from people, whether they give or refuse.
Gathering firewood isn't glamorous work. The saying treats it as honorable, because it's yours. Fourth, how Muslims hold this.
Earning a lawful living, halal, through honest work, is spoken of as part of faith. Muslims also give zakat, a required giving to people in need, and the hadith collections praise helping others.
These sayings don't look down on anyone who receives help.

teach.h: FROM THE WORK OF HIS OWN HANDS.
teach.b: They lift up the worth of honest effort, however humble: a person sitting down to bread they paid for with their own hands, and finding it tastes good.

how: Muslims speak of earning a halal, lawful living through honest work as part of faith, and teachers often cite the hadith of David eating from the work of his own hands.

o: a chapter of the Qur'an about David's armor
the collector of the Prophet's sayings

games.q: inside today's sayings — tap the pairs.
p: ate from the work of his own hands
better than begging, the hadith says

it calls carrying a bundle of firewood to sell better than begging from people.

games.q: you could ask for help today, or take a rope, gather firewood and sell it. what does the hadith in al-Bukhari say?
o: asking is always better than tiring work.
gathering and selling the firewood is better than begging.
games.why: the saying calls it better to carry a bundle of firewood on your back and sell it than to beg from people, whether they give or refuse.

practice: Think of the next thing you'll eat and trace it backward: whose hours paid for it, or, if you made it, the chopping, the stirring, the heat.
If someone else's hands paid for it today, a parent, a partner, a stranger at a shelter, hold them in mind with thanks, then look at your own hands for a breath or two.
If you pray, you can give thanks for your food in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Al-Bukhari, whose collection keeps the saying that no one eats better food than what they earn by the work of their own hands, as David did. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, from the Islamic tradition: the work of his hand, the phrase the hadith uses for what David ate from.

carryVoice: Your line: bread you paid for. Even a king kept a trade. Day eight hundred ninety-six counts.
